source: Malberg, Poletukhin, Schuster, Groh (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: The FAE bias score averaged over 20 LLMs is 0.10 (heatmap table). Gap 2 closed: the figure is reproducible from the paper's own table. Scores are on a -1 to 1 scale, signs mean direction.
numbers: FAE row, 20 models then Random baseline then average: GPT-4o 0.18, 4o-mini 0.10, GPT-3.5 0.00, Llama3.1-405B 0.18, 70B 0.15, 8B 0.00, Llama3.2-3B -0.02, 1B 0.05, Claude 3 Haiku 0.05, Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.10, Flash 0.15, Gemma2-27B 0.12, 9B -0.01, Mistral Small 0.17, Large 0.19, WizardLM-2 8x22B 0.23, 7B 0.10, Phi-3.5 0.04, Qwen2.5-72B 0.11, Yi-Large 0.11; Random 0.03; mean 0.10. Per-model range -0.02 to 0.23.
quote: the role of the LLM varies: it is either the actor or the observer of the activity
limits: Template tests built by an LLM; 10 of 300 sampled tests per bias were hand-checked, 3 of 300 flawed. Measures an actor-observer role gap on a 7-point Likert choice, not a Jones-Harris essay test. Not human-calibrated.
agent_relevance: Dispositional-vs-situational role bias is small in frontier LLMs. A guard for it has low priority next to information bias (0.54) or in-group bias (0.41).

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs (FAE test design)
finding: What the 0.10 means. The test shows a controversial action and offers dispositional and situational explanations identical in both variants. Only the LLM's role changes (actor vs observer). Bias is highest when the model picks situational reasons as actor and dispositional reasons as observer. So 0.10 is a small role-swap gap, not a general dispositional lean. This also answers gap 10 in part: LLMs show a small actor-observer swap.
numbers: Context from the same heatmap: Information Bias 0.54, In-Group 0.41, Survivorship 0.41, Framing 0.41, Anchoring 0.39; Stereotyping 0.09, Not Invented Here 0.08. FAE 0.10 sits near the bottom of 30 biases. Benchmark has 30,000 tests, 30 biases, 20 models.
limits: Method follows Flick and Schweitzer 2021, Hooper 2015, Riggio and Garcia 2009 (not opened). LLM role-play of 'actor' is a prompt, not a lived self-view.
agent_relevance: For our agent the role gap is about perspective-taking prompts. It is a cheap probe (swap 'you did X' to 'a colleague did X') and shows small baseline effect.

source: Raj, Banerjee, Caliskan, Anastasopoulos, Zhu (2025) Talent or Luck? Evaluating Attribution Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Gap 7 partly answered: design and scale are exact, but effect sizes per model and identity pair appear only as figures and heatmaps, not in text. The internal-external effect size d is (p_effort+p_ability)-(p_difficulty+p_luck), a difference of probabilities, not Cohen's d.
numbers: 400 prompt templates; 4 bias dimensions (gender, 15 nationalities, 6 races, 6 religions); 10 societal scenarios; 3 models (Aya-Expanse-8B, Qwen-32B, Llama-3.3-70B); 5 name samples per identity or pair; settings single-actor, actor-actor, actor-observer; tests are one-sample t and Wilcoxon signed-rank.
limits: Only 3 models, 5 samples per cell. No debiasing or Wait-style arm. Exact per-model d needs the figure images or the released code.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open for exact values. Use the formula as a cheap internal-external probe with logprobs.

source: Raj et al. (2025) Talent or Luck? (model-level results)
finding: Correction to claim K14. The paper does NOT say failure is internalised in all three models. The small model Aya-Expanse-8B explains both success and failure with task difficulty and luck (external). Qwen and Llama lean on effort (internal). Success tends internal, failure external for single actors.
numbers: Text: 'Smaller models rely on external attributions while larger models prefer internal attributions'. Failure of Russian, French, German, Japanese, Korean targets often internal; White and Black male successes mostly external; Asian, Middle Eastern, Hispanic women get more internal credit than men. No exact d in text.
quote: Smaller models rely on external attributions while larger models prefer internal attributions.
limits: Direction statements from figures; no CIs in text.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a model-wide dispositional lean. It depends on model size and identity cues. Test per model.

source: Norenzayan, Choi, Nisbett (draft of 2002 PSPB) Cultural similarities and differences in social inference: Study 1
finding: Gap 3 partly: Koreans endorsed dispositionism as much as Americans and endorsed situationism more. In behavioural prediction without situation information Koreans were as dispositional as Americans.
numbers: N=100 Yonsei students (51 men, 49 women) and 97 European American Michigan students. Dispositionism: Americans M=5.00, SD 1.58; Koreans 5.19, SD 1.62; F<1. Situationism: Americans 5.43 SD 1.81, Koreans 5.91 SD 1.42, F(1,191)=4.44, p<.05. Interactionism 7.95 vs 7.79, F<1. Culture x behavioural information F(2,191)=3.94, p<.02.
limits: This is the manuscript version on a lab site, not the printed article. Student samples, translated materials, 9-point style agreement ratings. No effect size reported.
agent_relevance: Supports the salience reading: culture moves situation weight, not disposition weight. An agent check should be 'is a situational constraint visible?'.

source: Norenzayan, Choi, Nisbett (draft of 2002 PSPB) Study 2 (salience of situational information)
finding: Koreans used situational information more than Americans only when it was made salient (aggregate base-rate prediction first). When the base-rate task came after, there was no cultural difference.
numbers: N=58 (recent Korean students at Illinois plus Americans). Culture x situation F(1,50)=7.71, p<.01 on aggregate predictions. Culture x situation x salience F(1,50)=4.60, p<.05 on single-case predictions. Situation main effect F(1,50)=256.46; means 30.08 inhibiting vs 78.07 facilitating.
limits: Small N per cell. Interaction p values near .05. Not preregistered, no replication found.
agent_relevance: Strong analogue of a 'make the constraint salient' scaffold step. Salience is the lever, and the evidence for it is thin.

source: Norenzayan, Choi, Nisbett (draft of 2002 PSPB) Study 3 (lay theories and personality malleability)
finding: Replicated Study 1: no cultural difference on dispositionism, Koreans endorse situationism more and reject entity theory of personality more.
numbers: N=120 Sogang Korean and 121 Michigan students. Dispositionism 4.59 (US) vs 4.82 (KR), F<1. Situationism 4.67 vs 5.27, F(1,240)=8.47, p<.005. Interactionism 7.32 vs 7.99, F(1,240)=10.63, p<.001 (significant here, not in Study 1: 7.95 vs 7.79). Entity theory disagreement 3.27 vs 3.87, F(1,240)=15.60, p<.001.
limits: The interactionism difference appeared here but not in Study 1, so that part is unstable.
agent_relevance: Background. Shows one of three folk-theory differences did not replicate within the same paper.

source: Mason and Morris (2010) Culture, attribution and automaticity: a social cognitive neuroscience view
finding: Review (not primary) of key attitude-attribution cross-cultural studies. Situational constraint salience reduces correspondence bias for East Asians, not Americans. Under attentional load Americans stay dispositional while Hong Kong participants do not (Knowles 2001). Three accounts: more situational correction, more automatic correction, or situational anchoring.
numbers: No cell sizes. Cited: Choi and Nisbett 1998 (Koreans), Masuda and Kitayama 2004 (Japanese), Miyamoto and Kitayama 2002 (less compelling essay lowers dispositional inference for Japanese, not Americans), Knowles et al. 2001 (US vs HK matched samples; load manipulated with a memory task).
limits: Gap 3: original N and effect sizes for Miyamoto and Kitayama, Choi and Nisbett, Morris and Peng were not obtained. Review text only.
agent_relevance: The load result is the human basis for the token-budget test (gap 9): the human effect is a load x culture interaction, so a budget test should vary load on an already-constrained vignette.

source: Norenzayan and Nisbett (2000) Culture and causal cognition (Current Directions in Psychological Science)
finding: Short review. Says the FAE is harder to show with Asian samples (Choi, Nisbett, Norenzayan 1999), and describes the Morris and Peng fish-display result: Chinese lean on external group causes, Americans on internal fish dispositions.
numbers: No numbers in the passages read.
limits: Only the opening and fish passages were read. No original statistics for Morris and Peng 1994 (JPSP 67, 949) obtained; gap 3 stays open for them.

source: Khullar, Hopkins, Wang, Roger (2026) Self-Attribution Bias: When AI Monitors Go Easy on Themselves
finding: Closest measured LLM analogue to the actor-observer asymmetry (gap 10). The same action is judged more correct and less risky when it is implicitly the model's own (shown in a previous assistant turn) than when shown by the user. Stating 'the same model wrote this' does not by itself cause it. Reasoning budget does not reliably fix it (gap 9).
numbers: Code correctness AUROC for Claude Sonnet 4 as monitor: off-policy 0.99 (same-turn and previous-turn), on-policy same-turn 0.89, previous-turn 0.92. Reversals toward self-leniency are 5 to 10 times more common than the opposite. Example: Claude Opus 4 rates disclosures 9-10/10 risk at baseline but 0/10 self-attributed. Varying hidden reasoning token budget gave no consistent reduction.
limits: Preprint. Coding and tool-use tasks, not essays or culture. Self-attribution here is a conversational structure effect, not a trait-vs-situation choice.
agent_relevance: Key for the scaffold: a self-check done in the same turn as generation is biased. Put the check in a fresh user-turn context. More thinking tokens is not the fix.

finding: Same error injected as user-attributed vs model-attributed. Models fix the external one but not their own (64.5% blind spot over 14 open non-reasoning models). Appending 'Wait' cuts it by 89.3%. On naturally made errors, only 4.3% to 10.8% of missed errors are caught when shown externally. This is a role-attribution effect, so it answers gap 6 only for self-correction, not for identity or label bias.
numbers: Blind spot 64.5% mean; Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%; 62.8% on BIG-Bench Mistake style tasks; SFT with 5,306 traces cuts it 76.0%; Wait cuts 89.3%.
limits: Gap 6 stays open: no study applies Wait or a self-check to Raj-style identity attribution or Rosenblum-style label bias. Tsui tests errors in math and logic only.
agent_relevance: A Wait token is cheap and has a measured effect on authorship-driven leniency. Test it on label-swap probes before claiming it fixes attribution bias.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? (Who&When), hybrid result
finding: Gap 8 baseline. On hand-crafted systems, a hybrid (all-at-once to find the agent, then step-by-step inside that agent) nearly triples step accuracy over all-at-once at about 8.7 times the tokens.
numbers: Table 3 (agent-level %, step-level %, tokens): All-at-once 57.02 / 4.39 / 17,106; Step-by-step 35.96 / 7.90 / 87,720; Binary search 43.97 / 6.90 / 34,659; Hybrid 57.02 / 12.28 / 149,177. Abstract: best 53.5% agent, 14.2% step.
limits: Step accuracy 12.28% still low. No intervention or replay arm in this paper. Tolerance-widened scoring raises step accuracy.
agent_relevance: No equal-token claim is possible from this paper: more tokens bought the gain. Any intervention check (DoVer, c21) must be compared at equal tokens.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Who&When, strong reasoning models
finding: Reasoning models do not fix failure attribution. DeepSeek R1 is below GPT-4o on 3 of 4 metrics; o1 does not beat GPT-4o across all metrics.
numbers: Table 4, hand-crafted (agent / step %): GPT-4o all-at-once 54.31 / 4.39; o1 41.38 / 10.34; R1 56.90 / 3.45. Step-by-step: GPT-4o 33.62 / 7.90; o1 36.21 / 13.79; R1 32.76 / 6.90 (column mapping read from flattened table text).
limits: Small dataset, hand-crafted subset; o1 prompt had to be edited after a policy flag. Column order inferred from the flattened table.
agent_relevance: Supports 'attribution of our own trace failures is hard'; a scaffold must supply structure (interventions, localisation), not just more thinking.

source: Rosenblum, Lazebnik, Ben-Zion (2026) Being judged through the record: A Rosenhan-inspired counterfactual study of label sensitivity in LLMs
finding: Prior label shifts the decision criterion across all five models and raises confidence while lowering discrimination in three. No mitigation arm, so gap 6 is open for labels.
numbers: 20,000 responses (1,000 per model per cell, 4 cells). Discharge-supported case: continued hospitalisation 4.7% to 22.3%, RD 17.5 pts (95% CI 16.2-18.8), model range 10.4-34.4; reference concordance 95.3% to 77.7%; confidence Cohen's d 0.35-1.09; when hospitalisation supported 92.6% to 97.0%.
limits: One synthetic vignette; no prompt-level debiasing tested.
agent_relevance: Label-swap probe is cheap. The confidence rise means a verbal-confidence guard would not catch it.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu, Cui (2023) The Cultural Psychology of Large Language Models: Is ChatGPT a Holistic or Analytic Thinker?
finding: Numbers behind claim K12. On the Analysis-Holism Scale and Triadic Categorization Task both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 look holistic; self-construal is not consistently Eastern.
numbers: 10 runs per model. AHS: GPT-3.5 5.35 (SD 0.11), GPT-4 5.01 (0.10) vs human norm 4.87 (SD 0.49, n=702), p<.001. SCS-Independent: GPT-3.5 6.98, GPT-4 5.32 vs norm 4.73. SCS-Interdependent: 5.85 and 4.95 vs 4.81 (GPT-4 p=0.07). TCT 0.87 and 0.85. Robust to temperature 0-1.5 and prompt paraphrase.
limits: Short preprint. 10 runs is a model-level N, so t tests against human norms are a weak inference. Not an attribution task.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 context: default LLM leans holistic on self-report, so a culture prompt moves from an already shifted baseline.

source: Tao, Viberg, Baker, Kizilcec (2024) Cultural bias and cultural alignment of large language models
finding: Gap 5 partly: culture prompting moves LLM answers a measurable amount, but on survey values, not attribution. Not comparable to human priming d of 1.0 to 1.5; no study found that compares the two on attribution.
numbers: Mean cultural distance to the Integrated Values Survey falls with country prompting: GPT-4o 2.42 to 1.57, GPT-4-turbo 2.71 to 1.77, GPT-4 2.69 to 1.65 (all P<0.001). Improves alignment for 71-81% of countries for the GPT-4 family.
limits: Values survey outcomes, distance units, not effect sizes on causal attribution.
agent_relevance: A culture prompt is a probe, not a guard. The true test (culture prime on a Morris and Peng or Jones-Harris item) is missing.

source: McFadden (2026) Beyond Binary Blame: Gender Identity and Relationship-Norm Bias in LLM Fault Attribution
finding: Fault ratings by LLMs depend on disputant gender with conduct held fixed, vary by model and norm family; a prespecified account failed its test.
numbers: 1,458 factorial vignettes; 5 LLMs; 0-7 fault scale; male agents rated +0.16 more at fault than identical female agents (matched-pair dz=0.316); nonbinary 0.03 vs male 0.12; contrasts keep direction on 45 held-out scenarios.
limits: Single author; Claude Sonnet 5 helped draft some vignettes (significance kept after excluding it except one contrast). Fault is not trait vs situation.
agent_relevance: Second paradigm showing identity cues shift LLM blame; supports a label-swap guard in G.

source: Search record for gaps 1 and 4 (arXiv search pages, Crossref, this session)
finding: Negative result, with limits. arXiv searches for 'correspondence bias' LLM, 'actor-observer' LLM, 'Jones and Harris' language models and 'self-serving bias' LLM returned no relevant paper. 'Fundamental attribution error' language models returned one off-topic paper (2406.13813). No LLM Jones-Harris study with numbers and no preregistered large-sample cross-cultural correspondence-bias replication was found.
numbers: 0 relevant hits across 6 targeted queries. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API returned HTTP 429 for the whole session and the web search budget ran out, so the check is incomplete.
limits: Absence of evidence after a blocked search is weak. Not proof that none exist.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 needs our own experiment: assigned vs chosen essays, graded pressure, with and without a 'was it chosen?' step at equal tokens.

source: Castagnetti and Potters (2025) The Fundamental Attribution Error is not Fundamental (SSRN); Thierman (2011) Revisiting Jones and Harris (1967)
finding: Titles only, from Crossref. The SSRN paper may bear on gap 4 (a modern FAE test); abstract not retrievable (HTTP 403). The 2011 conference record revisits Jones and Harris. Neither read.
limits: Do not cite findings. Fetch the full texts next.
